newsitem.title: PERU: American nations mull problems, dodge controversy.
newsitem.headline: American nations mull problems, dodge controversy.

text.p: The 34 nations of the Organisation of American States (OAS) wound down their 27th annual assembly on Thursday, continuing to steer a careful path round the Western Hemisphere's most intractable problems.

The region's most controversial and long-running issues, including the United States embargo on Cuba and Argentina's dispute with Britain over the Falkland Islands, were discussed briefly during the five-day conference in Peru.
But rather than take politically charged stances, the OAS merely "took note" of specific problems while issuing sweeping pledges to expand democracy and uphold human rights throughout the hemisphere.

Host country Peru created the biggest stir with an escalation of anti-government protests that saw police beating back a march on the assembly on Wednesday, and fighting a pitched battle with demonstrators outside Congress on Thursday.

The assembly's avoidance of controversy was exemplified by a resolution on Wednesday to "continue examining" Argentina's claim to sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, which it calls the Malvinas, where it went to war with Britain in 1982.

On another regional problem, the OAS inter-American legality committee condemned the U.S. Helms-Burton law tightening sanctions on Cuba as "not conforming with international law." But the full assembly voted only to "take note" of that ruling.

Peru again complained about mine-laying by Ecuador on the disputed border where the two countries went to war in 1995. And Bolivia reiterated its century-old claim to a sea access through Chile -- but to no avail.

"It is clear that the room and possibilities for multilateral action have their limits," Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar told reporters. "Rather than being the forum for resolving problems, the OAS is the place where the problem lives and is put on the table and the concern is made clear."

OAS officials tried to focus media attention at the assembly on a six-point Lima Commitment signed by foreign ministers that affirmed democracy and respect for human rights as "the fundamental elements of inter-American cooperation and solidarity."

The declaration also promised to step up the war on terrorism, corruption and trafficking of drugs and arms, but it contained few specifics on how to tackle these and made no reference to the blemished human rights and democracy records of some member nations.

OAS General-Secretary Cesar Gavira, however, was upbeat at Thursday's closing ceremony. "We close this assembly full of new enthusiasm ... in our possibilities that the future of America will be a future of prosperity, peace, equality and justice," he told delegates.

Despite the regional issues, it was Peru's internal problems that came under the most intense media spotlight. Wednesday's and Thursday's protesters, mainly students, workers and members of opposition parties, were challenging the government-controlled Congress' dismissal last week of three judges on the highest constitutional court who were blocking a third election bid by President Alberto Fujimori.

The protesters said the measure made a mockery of Peru's hosting a forum claiming to back democracy. The United States delegation, which kept a low profile at the assembly, emerged from the sidelines to condemn Congress' move as a "step backwards" in Peru's democratic process.
Gaviria skirted the issue as an internal matter but his inter-American committee on human rights gave an audience to the dismissed judges before formally registering its concern.
